title_original: Tanya Marcuse: “I apply gold to things in the world, but then photograph them”
excerpt_original: For eighteen months, Tanya Marcuse photographed the decomposing body of a deer, before transfiguring it: gilding it, giving it a heart. From that ritual came Deer, published by Roman Nvmerals and MW Editions, and an exhibition at CPW in Kingston, New York. L’article Tanya…

blocks.text: An American photographer born in 1964, Tanya Marcuse lives in the Hudson Valley, where she teaches at Bard College and creates in a tent-studio set up in her garden. There she assembles monumental tableaux inhabited by plants, flowers, and animal carcasses, some of which have long resided in her personal freezer, banished long ago from the family refrigerator. A Guggenheim Fellow, her work is held in the collections of the Met, SFMoMA, and the National Gallery in Washington. Deer , her latest book, marks a turning point, drawing the artist out of her usual domain and toward her subject. Interview.

blocks.caption: Deer Nº 7084 (2023-25). © Tanya Marcuse. Courtesy CPW, Kingston, New York.

blocks.text: You photograph Deer exactly as you photographed Woven : from directly overhead, on the same dark ground, with no horizon anywhere in sight. The subject has changed utterly; the vantage point hasn’t moved an inch. What does that horizontality allow you, and what keeps you faithful to it?

Tanya Marcuse : I love the idea of being faithful to horizontality (the way I’ve been miraculously faithful in my marriage). In both Woven and Deer , I remain committed to a horizonless frame, though the formal approaches differ somewhat. The panoramic proportions of Woven engage the viewer’s peripheral vision, while Deer , in a 4:5 aspect ratio, shifts between seeing the deer right-side up and upside down, occasionally introducing a slight angle between the ground and the camera. In both projects, I want an extreme sense of groundedness, looking down toward the earth, while at the same time being unmoored from the horizon, the world in the photograph pressed to the picture plane.

For Woven , you went out and gathered your materials, or they were brought to you: snakes, antlers, a pheasant. With Deer , it was you who traveled to the body. Why did you never move him? Was he simply impossible to carry, or was leaving him where he fell a decision? And what changed, practically, in going out to your subject rather than composing it at your own pace in your garden?
It’s a keen question. At first, moving the deer was unimaginable: its weight, the immediacy of its unfolding decay.

A year passed. Working periodically with the deer by the side of the road, exposed to passing cars, was uncomfortable. Its body had become so much lighter that I sometimes lifted it to wrap vines around it. I began contemplating moving it. I arrived one day with a large sheet of Plexiglas, thinking I might slide the deer onto it, load it into my car, and bring it home to work with in my outdoor studio.

A state trooper pulled over. I assumed I was in trouble (I always think I’m in trouble), but he told me he’d seen me there many times and wondered what I was doing. I showed him the deer and some photographs on my phone. When I said I was considering bringing it to my backyard, he tilted his hat down, looked at the deer, thought for a moment, and said, “It seems the deer should stay where it died.” I took his advice.
When the body finally disappeared in April 2025, an elliptical, dark absence remained on the ground. That empty space became part of the film.

blocks.text: You’ve said you “painted it gold.” How is that actually done? Brush, leaf, spray, out in the open air? Could you walk me through the method? And what were you after that day: to preserve him, to honor him, to ennoble him, to consecrate him?

Painting the deer gold was the first gesture that made me feel I might make something beyond the cliche of the roadkill photograph. I used a powdered gold tempera that becomes metallic when wet, along with (I confess) a little gold spray paint. Suddenly the deer looked like a statue, but the flies and maggots continued their work. It was utterly uncanny. Painting the deer began an ongoing process of attending to and transforming its body, suggesting something sacred and mythic in what might otherwise be seen as just another roadside corpse.

In the text that accompanies the photographs, you write: “But I bring you a new heart. It bleeds and burns and lights up your chest.” Are we to take you at your word? Was there an object, laid in that emptied chest? And in that text more broadly, where does the factual end and the imagined begin?

The short answer is yes. I brought the heart of another deer, photographed it with golden snakes coiled around it, and lit it on fire. The vignette is also part of the Deer film. There’s something devotional in this work, but also something transgressive. A little like Victor Frankenstein, with the hubris of trying to reanimate a dead creature.

The writing consists of fragments I wrote in the second person to the deer as the work unfolded. For me, fact and imagination aren’t opposing forces; they’re completely intertwined, as I hope they are in the photographs.

blocks.text: You hunt images like a field photographer; you cultivate like a gardener, sowing seed in your frame; you compose like a painter; you grade and terrace like a landscaper; you burn; you gather like an archaeologist; you read Dante like a scholar. In your work, where does craft end and the artist’s gesture begin?

I love this description. But I’m not sure I can distinguish where craft ends and art begins. Is gardening a craft or an art? I think of these things as completely entangled. The gestures, the materials, photographic technique, the processes of composing and tending are all part of the work. It’s a thrilling way to work.

You draw part of your inspiration from manuscripts you’re happy to name: the Augsburg Book of Miracles, the Voynich, the Hollar etching the antlers on your title page come from. Your work puts me in mind of an illuminator’s: gold, and text set alongside an image. Except that you go further, since you lay the gold on the matter itself. Does that comparison mean anything to you?

I like the idea of an expansion outward, from the intimate, contained world of a manuscript page into the messy matter of the world itself. I apply gold to things in the world, but then photograph them, transforming them again into pictures.

In Book III of Ovid’s Metamorphoses , Actaeon is turned into a stag: he keeps a man’s mind, loses the power of speech, and is finally torn apart by his own hounds, who fail to recognize him. What does that scene stir in you? In your own text you write: “You speak in maggots spilling from your mouth.” Are you, in some way, trying to give him his voice back?

The story of Actaeon is utterly harrowing. I think it speaks to the violence inherent in the divisions we make between ourselves and non-human creatures. I’m not trying to give the deer a voice, exactly. I unexpectedly found myself in a relationship with another creature, one that continued even beyond the boundary between the living and the dead. The maggots seemed to animate the deer’s body in a way that was profoundly unsettling and extraordinary.
There was something about being with this body, witnessing its unraveling, that brought me into contact with existential impermanence together with ecological vulnerability and loss.

blocks.text: Tanya Marcuse’s exhibition “Woven / Deer: An Ecological Tapestry” is on view through January 17, 2027, at CPW, 25 Dederick Street, Kingston, New York. Thursday through Sunday, 11am to 5pm. Free admission. Tanya Marcuse’s book , Deer , is published by Roman Nvmerals and MW Editions (October 2026).
